content.thinking:
I should avoid stating specific figures and keep things at the level of placeholders. I'm working through how to describe the fraud-hold symptom without overstating it—thinking about how the FraudHoldsHigh alert fired alongside a modest error-rate uptick, and how to phrase what shoppers actually experienced when their orders got flagged for review.

Building the causal chain: fraud-hold rates climbed and errors ticked up, traced back to a replica getting scheduled onto a different accelerator type (A100 instead of V100) because the pod spec didn't pin accelerator affinity, letting the scheduler place it inconsistently. I'm noting that the exact mechanism for why the model behaves differently on the new card is unconfirmed—only the correlation and the fix (pinning to V100, which stopped the rule from firing) are verified—so I need to flag that as an assumption rather than a settled fact, and list the missing accelerator pinning as a contributing factor.

I'm numbering new action items AI-3 and AI-4 after the existing ones: one to validate fraud scorer consistency across accelerator types before allowing heterogeneous deployment, and another to alert on accelerator mix or per-replica score divergence. For the executive summary I'm keeping it to placeholders for duration and error rate, and reminding myself to avoid writing out small counting words like "one" or "two" when describing cards.

action_items.item: Before allowing mixed accelerator types for the fraud scorer, compare its outputs on the A100 and V100 cards on a fixed test set, find why they differ, and record the acceptable difference.
Alert when replicas of a service run on different accelerator types, and track the fraud-hold measure per replica so a single divergent replica is visible quickly.

causal_chain.step: Users and the paging rule saw the fraud-hold measure jump from {series_before} to {series_while_broken} on average (peak {series_at_worst}) from {began}, with account page errors rising slightly (peak {errors_at_worst} against {errors_before} before).

The change began at the same minute a new replica (io-shop-7d9c4f8b6-x2k9p) started serving the fraud scorer on an NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-40GB card, while the other replicas ran on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB cards.

The replica landed on a different card type because the pods were held to no particular card, so the scheduler could place them on any available accelerator. No deploy, release or flag change accounts for it.

Holding the pods to Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB brought the service back to baseline and stopped the paging rule firing, which supports the card type as the cause. Why the model's output differs between card types is not shown by the record, so the chain stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: Nothing in the deployment constrained which accelerator type pods could be scheduled on, so a mixed fleet could form without any change being made. The pin applied during the incident is a mitigation and the permanent fix is still awaiting review.
The fraud scorer's output was never checked for consistency across accelerator types, so a model that answers differently on another card went unnoticed until production.
Detection was slow and indirect: the alert was raised at {alert_raised}, {alert_raised - began} after the onset, and nothing flagged that a replica had started on a different card type.

input.executive_summary: For {duration}, from {began} to {recovered}, the shop's fraud-scoring output drifted away from normal and a small share of account page requests failed (error rate peaked at {errors_at_worst}, against {errors_before} beforehand). No deployment or configuration change happened. A new copy of the service started on a different type of GPU than the others, and the fraud model gave different answers there. Argus restricted the service to the original GPU type, the measure returned to baseline, and a draft code fix was proposed for review.

got_lucky: The impact was small: errors rose only slightly and request latency and volume stayed at baseline, so the drift in fraud scoring was caught before it did wider harm.
went_well: Argus placed the onset correctly, recorded the replica's card type and ruled out deploys, releases and flag changes within seconds.
The mitigation was confirmed by the service returning to baseline and the paging rule going quiet, and a draft fix was proposed straight after.
went_wrong: The paging rule only fired after the onset had been under way for a while, and no signal pointed at the replica placement.
The fix is still an open draft, so until it merges the pin is the only protection.

input.root_cause: The service's pods were not held to a particular accelerator card, so a new replica was scheduled onto an NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-40GB card while the other replicas ran on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB cards. The fraud-scoring model on the new card answered differently, and the fraud-hold measure stepped up at the onset. The exact reason the model differs between card types was not established.
input.symptom: Fraud-hold scores drifted and some account pages failed
